text.access_note: Open public beach with no charge expected, but check the official site before you go in case anything near the beach club is restricted.
text.description: Matira Beach is the long, pale stretch of sand on the southern side of Bora Bora, and the lagoon here stays shallow a long way out, so you can wade in and keep your feet on the bottom well away from the shore. That shallow water is what makes it easy to photograph: the colour changes from clear pale green near the shore to deeper turquoise further out, and your phone picks that up well. The best-known picture here is the sunset over the lagoon. Guides point to the soft stretch of sand beside Bora Bora Beach Club as the place where the sun lines up straight ahead over the water, with the lagoon still shallow far out. Guides place the beach club at the western end of the beach, so check on arrival. They also say this spot fills up first in the last hour of light, so arrive early and claim a patch of sand. The beach as a whole gets busy from roughly 11am to 2pm, and parking fills quickly, so for clean, people-free frames come earlier or later in the day. Keep the horizon level, let the water take up most of the picture, and wait for a gap between walkers. If you have time, Matira Point is a good second stop for shallow turquoise water with the outer islets and Mount Otemanu in view.
text.geographic_location: Matira Beach is in the Matira area at the southern end of Bora Bora, along the lagoon shore. Guides place the beach club at the western end of the beach, so check on arrival.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops on Bora Bora, so head for the southern end of the island, the Matira area, and check which local transport options suit you. Parking fills quickly, so a drop-off may be easier. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether you want more water or more sky. Include a curve of wet sand or a few ripples in the foreground to lead the eye out to the sun. For a different view, Matira Point shows shallow turquoise water wrapping round the point, with the outer islets and Mount Otemanu behind. Check the exact spot on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours stay rich instead of washing out. As the light fades, try night mode only if you are holding the phone very steady. Take a Live Photo or two as the waves move, then choose the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Bora Bora Beach Club (western end of the beach, on the sand). The lagoon stretching out with the sun setting straight ahead over the water. From here you look out over the lagoon, with the sun setting ahead of you over the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, arriving well before the last hour of light because this stretch fills up first. For quieter pictures of the beach itself, avoid roughly 11am to 2pm.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sunset and the lagoon, as it gives the most natural view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sand and sky in one frame, and keep the horizon away from the edges so it does not bend. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a distant islet or a single swimmer against the glow.

spots.name: Vaitape
spots.label: Vaitape

text.access_note: Vaitape is a working village with public roads and shoreline, but for ferries, tours or any private land nearby, check the official site before you go.
text.description:
Vaitape is the largest settlement on Bora Bora, so it is a good place to photograph everyday life rather than resort scenery. It sits on the western side of the main island, looking across the western end of the lagoon. Mount Otemanu, the island's tallest peak, may be visible in the distance, and Mount Pahia is close by. Small islets mark the outer edge of the lagoon. These layers of water, village and mountain are what make a simple phone picture feel like Bora Bora.

A few facts help you read the scene. The area was first settled around the 9th century. During the Second World War it served as a military supply base. Today ferries run from here to Tahaa and Raiatea, and small boats cross the lagoon, so boats and ferries use the waterfront. The village is low and close to sea level, which means your views stay open across the water.

For photos, think in layers. Put something near you in the foreground, such as a boat, a mooring post or a palm. Then let the lagoon fill the middle and, if they are visible, the mountains close the top of the frame. Keep the horizon level, and wait a moment for a boat or a passer-by to give the picture some scale. Cloud can change quickly, so take a few frames over a couple of minutes.
text.geographic_location: Vaitape is on the western side of Bora Bora's main island, on the lagoon shore. It is the island's largest settlement, and the main road runs through it.
text.directions_text: There are no train, tram or bus stops to start from, so reach Vaitape along the main road or by the ferry or boat transfer that lands here. From there, walk east for about 5 minutes on foot to reach the subject. The phone icon on the map is about 330 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line so the sky and any peaks get most of the frame. Include a foreground object for depth. Keep the phone level so the water edge does not tilt. For a second version, zoom in to 2x or more and frame only the peak if it is visible above the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the clouds keep their detail. Try a Live Photo when boats are moving, then choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 330 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. Late afternoon sun should fall on the village from behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the village, the water and the mountain together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to a boat or the shoreline and want the whole bay. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the peaks or a boat on the lagoon.

spots.alt: Vaitape, Bora Bora: the largest settlement on Bora Bora. Photo spot

spots.name: Bora Bora Yacht Club
spots.label: Bora Bora Yacht Club

text.access_note: The club may be a private or customer-only waterfront, so check the official site before you go.
text.description:
Bora Bora Yacht Club is a waterfront subject, and the view of it works well as a simple lagoon scene: the club, the water and some sky. It is a relaxed, working-waterfront sort of subject rather than a grand monument, so the photo is about atmosphere. Think turquoise water, any boats that happen to be moored nearby and a bit of sky.

The phone icon on the map is about 160 m east of the subject. That distance helps. You can fit the shoreline and the water into one frame, and the club becomes the focal point rather than filling the picture. Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole scene, then try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the club and anything in front of it. If there is a good line of shore or a jetty, use it to lead the eye towards the club.

Keep your phone level using the gridlines, and put the horizon on a third of the frame rather than in the middle. Boats and people move, so take a few frames. Check the exact access to the waterfront on the day, as the club and its landing may be for customers only.
text.geographic_location: On the Bora Bora lagoon shore.
text.directions_text: The club is about 160 m to the west of that point, roughly 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the club on one of the thirds, with the water filling the foreground and the sky above. Use a jetty, shoreline or moored boat as a leading line if there is one. Take a 1x shot first, then a zoomed one for a tighter version.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the club to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks washed out. Switch on Live Photos or motion to catch boats and ripples, and take a few frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From here the club, the shoreline and the water should all sit in one view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be best, as the sun should be behind you and light up the club. Late afternoon would put the sun in front of you, so expect glare and silhouettes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full scene, then the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the club and any boats. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you can get close to the water's edge and want a lot of sky and lagoon.

spots.alt: Bora Bora Yacht Club, Bora Bora: a waterfront subject. Photo spot
